package_info.why_malicious: Versions 5.6.0 and 5.6.1 of xz Utils were intentionally backdoored to allow remote code execution via SSH, enabling unauthorized access to affected systems. The malicious code was inserted by a trusted maintainer after a prolonged social engineering campaign.

execution_context.file_location: m4 macro script and bash scripts in the xz tarball

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Custom m4 macros and bash scripts that unpack and deploy a maliciously crafted liblzma.o object file during the build process.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During build/install-time, the code unpacks and deploys a malicious liblzma.o object file into the build output, ensuring the backdoor is present in the final library.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Build scripts are used to introduce a binary payload (liblzma.o) not present in the source code, which is a classic supply chain attack technique.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal build scripts should only compile and link legitimate source files, not inject pre-built or obfuscated binaries.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some projects use pre-built binaries for performance, but this is rare and should be transparent.
key_indicators: Deployment of binary object files not matching source code

execution_context.file_location: liblzma.o (malicious object file in the built library)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Malicious code in liblzma.o that hooks into the SSH authentication process by redirecting RSA_public_decrypt@...plt to the backdoor code.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when SSHD loads liblzma, the code intercepts cryptographic operations (RSA_public_decrypt) and diverts execution to the backdoor, enabling remote code execution via specially crafted SSH authentication requests.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Intercepting cryptographic functions in a compression library is highly abnormal and enables unauthorized access.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: liblzma should only provide compression/decompression, not interact with authentication or cryptographic routines.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: None; such hooks are never legitimate in this context.
key_indicators: Presence of code paths only triggered by specific input patterns

attack_chain.action: Threat actor gains maintainer access and prepares malicious build scripts and object files.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is included in official xz releases.

attack_chain.action: Malicious xz tarballs (5.6.0/5.6.1) are published and distributed to Linux distributions.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victims install the compromised xz package.

attack_chain.action: During installation/build, the malicious build scripts deploy the backdoored liblzma.o.
attack_chain.leads_to: Backdoored library is present on the system.

attack_chain.action: When SSHD loads liblzma, the malicious code hooks into the authentication process.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker can trigger remote code execution via SSH.

behavioral_signatures: Build scripts that deploy or unpack binary object files not present in the source tree
liblzma or xz libraries that hook or redirect cryptographic functions
Unusual CPU usage or performance anomalies in SSHD after xz upgrade
file_indicators: liblzma.o with unexpected or obfuscated content
xz source tarballs with non-standard build scripts or macros
network_indicators: Unusual SSH authentication attempts that trigger code execution
Unexpected outbound connections from SSHD process (if attacker payload is used)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for xz versions 5.6.0 and 5.6.1. Inspect build scripts for unpacking or deploying binary object files. Analyze liblzma.so for unexpected function hooks or code paths. Monitor SSHD for abnormal CPU usage or authentication behavior. Use file integrity monitoring to detect unauthorized changes to liblzma or xz binaries.
